date.note: First published in German as Nachfolge in 1937. Long known in English as The Cost of Discipleship (the SCM Press translation, from 1948 onward); the critical English edition in the Dietrich Bonhoeffer Works series, translated afresh from the German critical edition, appeared as Discipleship (Fortress Press, 2003, DBWE volume 4). The year 1937 marks the German first edition.

summary: Discipleship (Nachfolge, 1937), long known in English as The Cost of Discipleship, is a theological treatise by the German Lutheran pastor and theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer. It is organized around a contrast between 'cheap grace,' grace treated as forgiveness dispensed without repentance or discipleship, and 'costly grace,' grace that calls a person to follow Christ, and it develops this through an extended exposition of the Sermon on the Mount; it was written during the German Church Struggle of the 1930s.
description:
Discipleship (German Nachfolge) is a book by Dietrich Bonhoeffer (1906-1945), a German Lutheran pastor and theologian of the Confessing Church, first published in 1937 and long circulated in English under the title The Cost of Discipleship. The critical English edition, freshly translated from the German critical edition, was published as Discipleship in the Dietrich Bonhoeffer Works series (Fortress Press, 2003, volume 4). Bonhoeffer wrote it out of his work directing the underground Confessing Church seminary at Finkenwalde and against the background of the German Church Struggle (Kirchenkampf), the conflict within German Protestantism over the alignment of the church with National Socialism.

The book opens with the distinction for which it is best known, between what Bonhoeffer calls 'cheap grace' and 'costly grace.' Cheap grace, in his account, is grace treated as a possession the church dispenses cheaply, the preaching of forgiveness without requiring repentance, grace without discipleship, grace without the cross and without the living Jesus Christ; he calls it 'the deadly enemy of our church.' Costly grace, by contrast, is 'the treasure hidden in the field' and 'the pearl of great price,' costly because it costs a person their life and grace because it gives that person the only true life; it is costly because it calls to discipleship and grace because it calls a person to follow Jesus Christ. Bonhoeffer ties grace inseparably to the call to follow, summarized in the often-quoted sentence, in the standard English rendering, 'when Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die.' The obedience of the disciple and the grace of Christ are, on his account, not opposed but bound together in the concrete act of following.

The central chapters develop this understanding through a sustained exposition of the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5-7), which Bonhoeffer reads not as an unreachable ideal or a set of general principles but as the concrete call of Christ to be obeyed in discipleship. He treats the Beatitudes, the call to be salt and light, and the 'extraordinary' demands of the sermon, on retaliation and love of enemies, as descriptions of the life of those who follow, and he resists readings that would soften these into mere dispositions or defer them. The later part of the book turns to the church as the community of those called, the visible body of Christ in which discipleship is lived. This entry attributes the 'cheap grace' and 'costly grace' distinction, the reading of grace as the call to follow, and the christological interpretation of the Sermon on the Mount to Bonhoeffer and to the work itself, and records the book's setting in the German Church Struggle as a matter of historical report, without endorsing or adjudicating its theological claims.
